question: When checking blood tests for primary hypothyroidism, which result do you expect to see?
explanation: Think of the pituitary gland as a boss trying to get a lazy thyroid to work. When the thyroid slows down, the boss shouts louder by pumping out extra TSH! So a high TSH level is the main clue for primary hypothyroidism. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h1)

question: A patient with untreated hypothyroidism will most likely show which sign?

options.C: Excessive weight loss despite high appetite

explanation: Thyroid hormones are like your body's engine speed. Without enough of them, everything slows down—giving you a low metabolic rate, weight gain, and feeling cold all the time. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h1)

question: Why do doctors usually choose levothyroxine over other options for thyroid replacement?

options.A: It contains both active and inactive hormones in variable amounts
options.B: It has a predictable potency and smooth onset of action
options.C: It is derived directly from animal thyroid glands
options.D: It acts much faster than synthetic triiodothyronine

explanation: Levothyroxine is lab-made and gives a steady, reliable daily dose. No nasty surprises or wild hormone spikes! [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h2)

question: How is desiccated thyroid extract different from synthetic levothyroxine?

options.A: Both thyroxine and triiodothyronine from animal sources
options.B: Non-hormonal plant extracts that stimulate the pituitary
options.D: Chemically altered molecules designed to bypass the liver

explanation: Desiccated thyroid comes from dried animal glands, meaning it naturally carries a mix of thyroid hormones rather than just one lab-created formula. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h2)

question: Roughly how long is the plasma half-life of levothyroxine in a healthy person?
explanation: Because it hangs around in the body for about a week, patients only need to take it once a day. But it also means it takes a few weeks to adjust when a dose is changed! [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h3)

question: Why do nurses always tell patients to take levothyroxine on an empty stomach?

options.A: Food neutralizes the stomach acid needed to activate the tablet
options.B: Food and certain minerals in the gut can reduce the drug's absorption
options.C: The drug causes severe stomach ulcers if mixed with food proteins
options.D: Taking it with food causes immediate destruction of the liver

explanation: Things like calcium, iron, and heavy meals can trap the drug in your gut and stop it from getting into your bloodstream where it's needed. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h3)

question: Why must older adults or heart patients start levothyroxine at a very low dose?

options.A: Because high initial doses cause permanent damage to the thyroid gland
options.B: To prevent sudden increases in metabolic demand that could stress the heart
options.C: Because older adults absorb the medication much faster than young adults
options.D: To prevent the kidneys from excreting the drug before it works

explanation: Revving up the body's metabolism too fast is like slamming the gas pedal in an old car—it puts too much strain on the heart and can trigger chest pain. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h4)

question: A patient asks when is the best time of day to take their prescribed levothyroxine tablet. What is the correct response?

options.A: At bedtime right after a heavy meal to avoid daytime stomach upset
options.B: In the morning on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before eating
options.C: With lunch to help digest the afternoon meal more efficiently
options.D: Anytime during the day as long as it is taken with a cup of coffee

explanation: Morning dosing on an empty stomach ensures maximum and consistent absorption without interference from food or beverages. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h4)

question: What signs tell you that a patient is taking too much levothyroxine?

options.A: Dry skin, lethargy, and facial swelling
options.C: Slow resting heart rate and severe constipation
options.D: Extreme fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance

explanation: Too much hormone pushes the body into overdrive. It's like flipping from hypothyroidism straight into hyperthyroidism symptoms! [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h5)

question: Which of these common items can block your body from absorbing oral levothyroxine?
explanation: Minerals like calcium and aluminum act like magnets in your stomach, grabbing onto the levothyroxine and stopping it from entering your blood. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h5)

question: How often do doctors usually check TSH levels when figuring out the right levothyroxine dose?

options.A: Every single day before the morning dose
options.C: Every six to eight weeks until stable
options.D: Every twenty-four hours in the acute ward

explanation: Because the drug takes time to build up and settle in the body, doctors wait 6 to 8 weeks before checking the blood to see if the dose is spot on. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h6)

question: A patient says, 'I feel great now, so I want to stop taking my thyroid pills.' What should you tell them?

options.A: Explain that hormone replacement is usually a lifelong therapy needed to maintain normal body function
options.B: Agree that the thyroid gland has successfully healed and the medication is no longer necessary
options.C: Tell the patient to switch to herbal remedies since synthetic hormones are no longer required
options.D: Suggest cutting the pill in half to see if symptoms return before stopping completely

explanation: Remind them kindly: you feel great *because* of the pills! Stopping the medication means the low-thyroid symptoms will just come back. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T2#GNS223_U7_T2_h6)
